speaker: Other
text: Hearing hearing the Court of Appeals for the 1st District of Texas is now in session. Pursuant to adjournment, God save the Constitution and its honorable court.

speaker: peterkelly
text: Good afternoon and welcome to another virtual convention of the Court of Appeals for the 1st District of Texas. We have one case on the docket today for oral argument. Case number 01-20-00641-CV, State of Texas v. Cal-Maine Foods Inc., DBA, Wharton, and Wharton County Foods, LLC. Can we have the appearance of counsel on behalf of the appellant, State of Texas?

speaker: benwilson
text: Benjamin D. Wilson on behalf of the state, your honor.

speaker: peterkelly
text: And on behalf of the appellees?

speaker: craigstanfield
text: Your honor, Craig Stanfield on behalf of the Cal-Maine defendants.

speaker: peterkelly
text: And Mr. Wilson, are you going to reserve time for rebuttal? Yes, your honor. I'd like to keep five minutes for rebuttal. Five minutes for rebuttal. Okay, well, as soon as we move Mr. Stanfield off the screen, you may begin, Mr. Wilson.

speaker: benwilson
text: Thank you, your honor. May it please the court. Cal-Maine raised prices on eggs by 300% during a declared disaster, knowing that buying was panic-driven. The district court erred in every respect when it dismissed the state's complaint, seeking to hold Cal-Maine accountable for that price gouging. Section 1746.46B12 is not unconstitutionally vague. It does not violate the Dormant Commerce Clause. There's no regulatory taking, and Cal-Maine's grab bag of other arguments fail. At a minimum, judgment under Rule 91A was inappropriate because there are numerous questions back throughout this case. If Cal-Maine's right, then neither the state nor Texas may have recourse in a disaster to prevent, for example, a gas station from charging $12 a gallon for gas during a hurricane, or for a grocery store to charge $10 for bread or water during a winter storm that are declared as disasters. Go ahead, your honor, please.

speaker: amparoguerra
text: Thank you, Mr. Wilson. So is there a difference between those scenarios that you just mentioned where a particular gas station is overcharging for a gallon of gas versus a distributor who is following market pricing? In your example, are you meaning that we're talking about one particular gas station charging more than all the other gas stations in the area?

speaker: benwilson
text: It could certainly apply to either. Your honor, I think what that runs to is sort of some of the arguments at the back of their brief, talking about the state can't bring these claims because they're not a consumer. We have several arguments on that point. I think the most straightforward one is there's a separate statutorily available action for the state to bring, and the legislature created a separate cause of action for consumers. So we just don't think the consumer bar applies to the state when the state brings an action. The state has to, for example, show public interest, and there would have been no point for the legislature to create sort of separate actions if the state was bound by the consumer standard.

speaker: peterkelly
text: Let's talk about the price of eggs. Was there any other distributor besides CalMain charging three dollars a dozen?

speaker: benwilson
text: Your honor, I think that in the complaint we said that the price of eggs generally rose in Texas. I believe we said they have 90 percent of the growing facilities in Texas. I don't think that matches on perhaps entirely to how many that they're distributed or that they're distributing in Texas. But we also did allege that they're the I don't think we put a number to it in terms of sort of distributor sales,

speaker: peterkelly
text: but we certainly allege they're the dominant seller in the state. All right. So if they're the dominant seller, what was the price of eggs in Oklahoma?

speaker: benwilson

text: Egg prices rose nationwide and CalMain's prices rose while those egg prices were rising nationwide. I think that's right. So what do we look to to see what the price of eggs was?

speaker: benwilson
text: Well, we in the in the record, we have what the price in our complaint, we have what the price of eggs was immediately before immediately before the disaster was declared. text: Would it be fair to characterize that as the industry standard price?

speaker: benwilson
text: You know, your honor, I think whether that's an industry standard price is itself a question of fact. I think they certainly say it's an industry standard price. But I don't I certainly wouldn't quibble with the court that that is a price that may be relevant for purposes of proceedings.

speaker: peterkelly
text: So what is our inquiry when we're trying to determine whether the three dollars a dozen is exorbitant or excessive? Do we look at historical data or going back to 2010 or 1900 or whatever? Or do we look horizontally and look at what the prices were in, say, the Dallas market or in Oklahoma or California or New York?

speaker: benwilson
text: Well, your honor, I think what you would look to the statute also includes includes taking advantage of a disaster. So I think what you would look to is the price before the disaster. You would. So there are a couple of sort of inquiries there. One is whether the price was excessive. Where was this disaster? You know, I there is certainly a disaster declared in Texas. I imagine there there were also federally declared disasters. I imagine many other states declared. That's probably a worldwide disaster. I two years and I wouldn't fight with you on that point.

speaker: peterkelly
text: Right. So it's not a situation where, say, a hurricane has flooded Houston and people are bringing in the eggs that they're buying for a dollar a dozen in Dallas and selling them for three to three dollars a dozen in Houston.

speaker: benwilson
text: Correct. I think that's right, your honor, except I would point out that we do have allegations in the complaint about what the input costs were. That's that's driven both from their public SEC filings and and, you know, other things that that Calmain has said without discovery. And those filings say that they did not have the sort of input costs that you would expect it to rise to rise.

speaker: gordongoodman
text: Just for a second. Do you think that the their cost is significant in determining whether or not they engaged in price gouging in this situation?

speaker: benwilson
text: I think it's I think it's certainly relevant, your honor. I mean, I think I think the sort of test is we set out in our brief discusses, you know, what the price was before the what the price was before the disaster discusses whether that price would be would be a price that you could charge without losing business absent disaster. I think how I think really how these sort of input costs and things like that might become relevant is as a question as a question of that past the 91 stage. So, for example, if what you could show with evidence was, well, gosh, because we had to take all of these precautions because of the coronavirus or because our supply chains were deeply disrupted or because the price of feed went way up or something like that. I don't think you'd be taking advantage of the disaster if you could just say, well, look, my prices rose and I pass those prices on to my customers. I think if your prices go up 300 percent because there's panic buying in the market or people people think they really need eggs because of the disaster as well.

speaker: gordongoodman
text: None of that information is available at this early stage of the proceeding, is it?

speaker: benwilson
text: That's precisely correct, your honor. And that's why that's a large part of why we think that dismissal pursuant to Rule 91A was not appropriate.

speaker: peterkelly
text: So conceptually, let's say, I mean, we're going to factor in the input costs. Let's go back to 1973, right, where OPEC has a has an embargo on the United States. Price of oil hits the price of gasoline. It's a dollar a gallon at the pump. And and let's say Mobil has more efficient production methods than Gulf does. And so Mobil's production, you know, at a dollar, you know, the unconscionable price of a dollar a gallon, Mobil's making more of a profit than Gulf is. Is Mobil, under your scenario and your analysis, price gouging by taking advantage of a of a national crisis?

speaker: benwilson
text: Well, to be clear, your honor, I think that the things like input costs might become relevant as a factual defense. I don't I don't think that they're sort of relevant to the prima facie showing the state has to make a Rule 91A. I think what the state has shown Rule 91A is that there's a declared disaster. And we're taking advantage of it by charging excessive resorting prices and that the way that then cashes out.

speaker: peterkelly
text: Well, doesn't the state allege that CalMaine was charging the market price for the eggs?

speaker: benwilson
text: Yes, your honor. But as we point out in our brief, it can't just be that if everyone is because everyone is charging the same price, that means everyone can price gouge. I mean, the intuition here is, I think, really straightforward that the legislature determined. You know, we usually we usually charge. We usually sort of allocate scarce goods and resources in the United States by market price. There are certainly other ways to do it. You can form a queue. That's you know, we quickly call that first come first serve. It's also the case that, you know, sometimes you limit sometimes businesses limit the number of the number of something people can buy.

speaker: peterkelly
text: I'm having trouble conceptually with the idea that charging the market price, the industry recognized market price is price gouging.

speaker: benwilson
text: Oh, well, your honor. What I mean to say is, is this. In the in the context of a declared disaster where, for example, demand may skyrocket or demand may be particularly inelastic because people really need something. The legislature has made a policy determination that we're going to we're going to allocate these things other ways other than the market pricing mechanism.

speaker: peterkelly
text: Has it made that determination? I mean, it says exorbitant or excessive. I mean, if it's not exorbitant compared to the market, to the national market, how is it exorbitant?

speaker: benwilson
text: Well, your honor, we think we think that it's exorbitant or the correct test is exorbitant or excessive in relation to the price charge before the disaster. And sort of whether what was the peak price for a dozen eggs prior to the disaster? You know, I think it's certainly in the record that prices fluctuate. I believe the price right before the disaster was something like 94 cents.

speaker: peterkelly
text: Well, that's not what I asked. I asked was what was the peak price?

speaker: benwilson
text: In history, I they certainly say that they had approached three dollars at other times in the past. And that was because of things like and I think we talked about this in our complaint to things like. Flues, things like that that decrease flocks and cause prices to raise, but it's a very different situation here where none of that's where none of that's occurred.

speaker: peterkelly
text: I mean, that's because the market reacts to both supply and demand. And if there's a market price that is has gone up because demand is increased as opposed to supply decreasing, it's still the market price.

speaker: gordongoodman
text: I think you're talking about the percentages that other states have used to indicate excessive or exorbitant prices. My memory is that there were some that have specific red lines. Kentucky had about a 10 percent increase from the price prior to the the disaster and went up to about 25 percent, I think, in Maine and a few others. So in the 10 to 25 percent range was sort of deemed to be excessive or exorbitant as a matter of kind of presumption. And here we're talking about what, a 300 percent increase prior to the disaster declaration to just after the disaster declaration. Is there any other state that has a 300 percent threshold?

speaker: benwilson
text: Your Honor, the the numbers I'm aware of are the numbers that were are the statutes that we cited in the brief. I think there's range somewhere from like 10 percent to 25 percent. The point we're making with that, I think, is exactly what you're picking up on is that, you know, whatever whatever the whatever the price increase was or whatever price increase would be available or would be lawful. 300 percent is far outside, far outside the realm of those price increases.

speaker: amparoguerra
text: So if the entire industry is charging these market prices, then why is this selective enforcement against one particular producer as opposed to sort of an industry wide prosecution?

speaker: benwilson
text: Sure, Your Honor. A couple of points on that. First, you know, this Calmain is the dominant producer and seller in Texas. And so in a world where the state has has limited resources that it can use to investigate these things, to bring cases, it's completely it's completely normal and rational for the state to only bring some cases and sometimes only to bring cases against the biggest players.

speaker: peterkelly
text: What about the beef industry? Did beef go up in price?

speaker: benwilson
text: Your Honor, my understanding is that I will tell you, I'm not sure that it's in the record, but I eat a fair amount of beef. So I think beef prices have sort of famously gone up and that it's also widely reported what the what the challenges with supply chains and things like that in that industry have been. As I pointed out earlier, the beef producers taking advantage of the disaster by raising their prices. Well, I think if I think if the state brought such a claim, they might have fact they might have factual. The state hasn't brought that claim. The state did bring such a claim. They might have factual they might have factual defenses related to, you know, are we had to have lots of folks. Lots of folks were out. We had to have lots do spend lots of money on COVID protocol or supply chains or mess, things like that.

speaker: peterkelly
text: Any other questions from the panel? Thank you very much for your time, Mr. Wilson. And we'll hear from Mr. Stanfield. And because Mr. Wilson went over, we'll give Mr. Stanfield an extra three minutes if he wants it.

speaker: craigstanfield
text: Your Honor, I'm entirely at your disposal. May it please the court. Now, Maine follows the prevailing third party market index to set the price for its generic shell eggs. As the state admits, that pricing was true both before and after the governor's declared disaster declaration. As a result, Calmain continued to charge the ordinary and customary price for its eggs. And it is also true that Calmain did not change its pricing methodology in order to take advantage of the declared disaster.

speaker: gordongoodman
text: Are you saying that's a perfect defense? Let's assume that the price had gone not to three dollars, but two hundred dollars. Would that have been OK for you to charge one hundred dollars?

speaker: craigstanfield
text: Your Honor, if that was the published market price as it was nationally, then under A.B. Smalls and Cohen, we would be entitled to charge that price without being subject to this.

speaker: gordongoodman
text: And you don't think that would be exorbitant or excessive?

speaker: craigstanfield
text: Your Honor, if that were the normal customary price that flows out of the pricing formulas from the Erner-Berry index, then yes, that would be the ordinary customary price that would not have changed in order to take advantage of the disaster. The state needs to show two things. First, that we charge something different than our ordinary pricing formula. We are not the price setters. We take the prices published in the index. The second thing the state has to show is that we changed pricing methodology in order to take advantage of the disaster. Do we have the contract in front of us? No, Your Honor. The record talks about it for our investor presentations and that we have long term supply agreements with our retailers. But we don't have the contract in front of us to look at, do we? No, Your Honor. But you have paragraphs five and twenty nine of the state's petition where the state admits on the face of its petition that grocers, retailers, that those who actually sell the individual consumers price, according to Erner-Berry, and they purchase from us, according to Erner-Berry.

speaker: gordongoodman
text: Do you think it would be helpful for us to see the contract and making this determination?

speaker: craigstanfield
text: No, Your Honor. In light of the state's admission on the face of its petition, that that guides and that and what the state relies on in that petition guides what this court uses to to rule on this rule. Ninety one a appeal. The court does not need the contracts to affirm the decision below.

speaker: amparoguerra
text: But what's your response to their position that this is not necessarily proper for a ninety one a motion and that discovery should be had for the contracts and any other relevant information?

speaker: craigstanfield
text: Your Honor, my response to that is that we need only read what the state chose to put in its petition, which happens to be true, which is that the entire retail industry, whether it's Sam's, Costco, Publix, ATV, that they buy according to the Erner-Berry index and that we as Calmain sell to those retailers according to the Erner-Berry index. That's on the face of the petition. There's no fact finding that needs to be done. We agree with that. They've alleged that they have to live with that. Furthermore, Your Honor, you can look at anything that the state has quoted from or cited to in its petition as well. But again, I think if you look at paragraphs five and twenty nine of the state's petition, it fully resolves the questions we're talking about now, which is, did Calmain charge the Erner-Berry prices? And the state admits that we did both before and after the disaster declaration at issue in this case.

speaker: gordongoodman
text: Is there a force majeure provision in the contract?

speaker: craigstanfield
text: Your Honor, I'm not aware as to whether there is, and we don't believe that would impact the resolution of this appeal. Because again, Calmain, and this is in the state's petition, Calmain is not a price setter. Calmain's prices go up and down and half historically based upon what the published index says the price is. And this is in the record as well. So in twenty eighteen, when there was no disaster declaration, prices were at or above three dollars. The next year in twenty nineteen, they fell to sixty four cents. They were also at three dollars in twenty fifteen because of the avian flu.

speaker: gordongoodman
text: So you think that people should do exactly what they do in ordinary times when we're in the middle of a declared disaster emergency, is that right?

speaker: craigstanfield
text: Your Honor, this isn't a policy determination that we're putting forward. What we're saying is that regardless of how we believe the statute is void, void for vagueness on its face. But if the court were to apply a meaning to the statute, then the state has to meet two different tests. One, they have to show that we charged a price that was not ordinary and customary. And second, they have to show that that price was charged in order to take advantage of the disaster.

speaker: gordongoodman
text: I thought it was one sentence, not two sentences. I'm just looking at the statute doesn't appear to be two sentences to me.

speaker: craigstanfield
text: Your Honor, whether it's one sentence or two sentences, it's got multiple clauses. Read it if you'd like. I have it as well, Your Honor. And what I'm saying is that when we look at .46B27, it has subject to 4625 that you have to take. It's taking advantage of the disaster declared by the governor under Chapter 418, et cetera, by and then it has subsections A and B. So it does have multiple parts. And all of that language has to be accorded meaning. Otherwise, it's rendered mere surplusage. And so the state's reading of taking advantage, you could, under the state's reading, completely take that phrase out. And the statute would mean exactly the same thing as the state interprets it. And that's something that the court can't do when it's interpreting statutory text. And so on the face of this statute, though, and I want to go to your questions, Justice Kelly, the national market prices were essentially the same. They were over $3. And those prices are charged to Sam's, Costco, Walmart, HEB, Publix, Aldi, et cetera, pegged to those market indices. And so when we are confronted with this statute and with the statute and all of the case in all of the states around the country that have statutes that have, as you point out, Justice Goodman, varying levels of enforcement, whether it's 10 to 25 percent, 19 states have exceptions and defenses when you have a volatile market and you follow the market. Multiple states have exemptions altogether for agricultural goods. And so when we're confronted with a statute that does not provide us with a clear benchmark against which we can judge our prices, then we run headlong into a vagueness problem. Because as the statute is written, the prices don't even have to change. On the face of the statute, it only requires that at the time of the declared disaster, that a fact finder determine those prices are exorbitant or excessive. So you can have exactly the same price. And the state lauds this alleged flexibility on page eight of its opening brief, where it says that plaintiffs have great flexibility in determining how to bring the case. But that is exactly the wrong way the statute should be interpreted. Because as a penal statute, and the one that implicates our right to interstate commerce, it has to be narrowly construed. And we have to be able to judge what is in and out of bounds under the statute. And the two cases that are most on point we think for us are A.B. Smalls and Cohen. Those are two cases that dealt with the sugar market in the early 1920s. And those cases were reaffirmed by the United States Supreme Court in Johnson versus United States in 2015. And with those cases stated, to go straight to your point, Justice Goodman, in those cases they stated, we understand that surely someone could bring an example to us like $1,000 for a bag of sugar and say that this is unjust, unreasonable, or excessive, which was the language of that statute. But simply because we can find examples that would clearly meet the statute's definition does not save it from a constitutional standpoint. And there it was struck down, both under the criminal and the civil versions of those statutes. So we think those cases are most on point. Similarly, under Johnson versus United States, in 2015, a much more recent Supreme Court struck down the Armed Career Criminals Act, even though over Justice Alito's dissent, they said we could find examples where this statute applies. But there's so much unknown that we can't. Justice Kalasi, you're leaning in.

speaker: peterkelly
text: Actually, I was getting a sip of water.

speaker: craigstanfield
text: Oh, okay. I wanted to be respectful if you wanted to ask a question. Go ahead, Justice Guerra. I'm sorry.

speaker: amparoguerra
text: I was going to ask, so what's the difference between this and, for example, the Sherman Act that also is very vague in its delineations?

speaker: craigstanfield
text: I really know. Sorry, say what? Or the Clayton Act? I really appreciate those questions. So in fact, the Supreme Court dealt with those in the Cohen and Small decision. Because in 1913, in the Nash decision, the Supreme Court upheld the antitrust statutes. Part of the reason why they distinguished upholding the antitrust statutes but striking down the price control statutes during World War I was because those antitrust statutes incorporated into themselves a tremendous amount of common law that then people had something by which to gauge their conduct. There was an expansive body of law that they could go to to say, this would be in and this would be out. But as the court said, the sugar... Go ahead, Justice Kelly.

speaker: peterkelly
text: Do the contracts require the Cal-Maine to refer to the Erner-Berry pricing market?

speaker: craigstanfield
text: Yes, Your Honor. Much like the oil and gas market has for long term supply agreements, although they rely on NYMEX or Platts, the pricing with our large retailers is either a premium or a discount over a regional index. I do want to highlight on that for just a second. For Texas, Texas is in the south central region of Erner-Berry. It is not a only market. This is a market set by multiple states and we think that's important to our dormant commerce clause argument. But to answer your question specifically, there is a spot market where people can buy and sell based upon that pricing. But there are also long term supply contracts that say, for example, we will buy at south central less 2 cents or 5 cents or maybe they'll pay a premium to it. Again, that's not necessary to resolve this appeal, but that is how the market works.

speaker: peterkelly
text: But we don't have those contracts in front of us, do we?

speaker: craigstanfield
text: No, Your Honor, and you don't need them.

speaker: peterkelly
text: I understand your argument is we can just refer to paragraphs 5 and 29 of the state's complaint. But setting that aside, we don't have the contracts in front of us right now.

speaker: craigstanfield
text: That's right, Your Honor. What you have is the state's admission that CalMain, both before and after the disaster declaration, which incidentally still runs today, has always charged the market prices to its customers who are not end-use consumers.

speaker: peterkelly
text: Could CalMain have charged, say, $5 a dozen?

speaker: craigstanfield
text: Your Honor, no. For two reasons. One, that's not the Erner-Berry index. It never reached that price. And as the state also admits in its petition, our customers, even under long-term agreements, are fully able to enter the spot market. So when Erner-Berry is at $3 and we offer a $5 price, then no, we won't be able to sell those eggs. That's simply not the market price. And we do not have captive customers. For example, Justice Guerra, I think you touched on this. This is very different than a situation where someone may be on a highway and there may be one gas station next to them and not another one that they can get to. In that case, that gas station has a captive market. That's not the situation here. And in fact, what the state seems to allege, although it's not supported by their pleading, is that maybe they wish they had brought some sort of antitrust claim. Maybe they wish they brought a different claim. But we do not control the market. The state does not allege that we control the market. And in fact, what the state alleges and admits is that we are one part of a very volatile fragmented egg market that simply follows the market prices when they go up and when they go down. But in effect, what the state would have the DTPA do here is work extraterritorially. Because these are prices that are entered into by CalMain with national retailers to govern national contracts. And again, those prices change automatically based upon the index. But in effect, and the state concedes this, given the patchwork of state laws out there that govern price gouging, if they all were to be invoked at the same time as they were here, then our only other option is to find the most restrictive statute and follow that pricing, presumably for two years and however long the pandemic goes on, that our prices can never change. There is no exception or defense in the DTPA for increased cost of goods. There's no exception or defense in the DTPA for market changes in prices. There's no exemption for agricultural goods. And as the record here demonstrates, prices over the last 10 to 15 years have fluctuated from $0.55 to over $3. And they've hit the $3 mark three times, avian flu 2015, the retail wars in 2018, and then the pandemic for only three weeks before they fell again down to around $1 for a dozen eggs.

speaker: amparoguerra
text: So in the states that have the more restrictive, for example, the 10% rule, do you sell at a different price in those states?

speaker: craigstanfield
text: Your Honor, our position, wherever we are, is that we follow our contract. Because again, we are not changing our pricing in order to take advantage of the disaster, one. And two, because we don't sell to individual consumers. We always sell to retailers. So someone coming to us individually saying I want a dozen eggs, we don't sell to those individuals. And the way the vast majority of price gouging statutes work is you have to sell to an individual consumer buying for home or personal use. It does not reach conduct between sophisticated businesses, which is what the state is trying to do here. All right.

speaker: gordongoodman
text: I didn't really hear an answer to Justice Guerra's question. But Kentucky has a 10% limit, if I remember correctly. Were you saying that you didn't increase prices by 300% in Kentucky?

speaker: craigstanfield
text: So, Your Honor, just as a minor point, first of all, under Kentucky, we followed the market because Kentucky has an exemption and a defense when you're using a preexisting price formula or contract. So our conduct was not prohibited by the Kentucky statute. And second, although maybe a bit pedantic, going from $1 to $3 is actually not a 300% increase as the state alleges. It's a 200% increase. I do acknowledge that's still larger than 10%. But taking the Kentucky statute on its face, we have an absolute defense under that statute because we're following a preexisting price formula and contract.

speaker: amparoguerra
text: But you admit that we don't have that same defense here in the DGPA.

speaker: craigstanfield
text: And that's what causes the dormant commerce clause problem for the state of Texas. On the face of the statute, and I understand the state would like this court to read language into the statute to limit it. But on the face of the statute, the state can govern pricing conduct wherever it occurs, as long as it directly or indirectly affects the Texan. So, for example, if a price is entered into between a Mississippi egg company like Cal-Maine and an Arkansas company like Walmart, but those eggs end up in Texas at a heightened price, then that contractual arrangement is going to be subject to up to $250,000 per violation by the state if it affects someone over the age of 65 in Texas. And that's precisely the dormant commerce clause problem here, just as it was in Frosch and in Healy, because we have a patchwork of different states' laws that when put together, make it such that you have to follow the most restrictive price out there if you want to be in compliance.

speaker: gordongoodman
text: I'm sorry, was there a claim for damages in this case, or just a claim for civil penalties?

speaker: craigstanfield
text: So they have alleged civil penalties and disgorgement. This is a classic penal context where the claim for relief that they have is unrelated to the actual damage or harm to an individual. And because it is a claim for penal damages, that is why this court, under binding case law, has to narrowly construe the statute in a way that benefits those who are governed by the statute. And we think that's an important point, because this statute doesn't just govern commercial actors. It governs any person who may sell a product of any sort that falls under their statute's purview, which is quite broad, as long as that conduct directly or indirectly affects the Texan. And so you could have, to use the state's language, a mom and pop who thinks, well, right now this is what the price is, this is what the price is nationally for this product. The governor declares a disaster, and that mom and pop organization on the corner has to decide, is my price now exorbitant or excessive? Now, the way that we believe the statute should be read, if the court can find a constitutional reading, is that they should not be punished, in part because if they don't change their pricing in order to take advantage of the disaster, if they're following their ordinary and customary pricing, then that should not be violative of the DTPA here. And your honors, I'm happy to answer any other questions that you have, but I also want to be respectful of your time.

speaker: peterkelly
text: Any other questions from the bench? Thank you very much, Mr. Stanfield, and now we will return to Mr. Wilson.

speaker: benwilson
